i0: We use the **present perfect** (*have / has* + past participle) to connect the past with **now**: *I**'ve lost** my keys* (I can't find them now). *She**'s been** to Japan three times* (in her life, up to now).
i1: The important thing is not **when** it happened but that it matters **now**. If you say when (*yesterday, in 2020*), use the past simple. See [Present Perfect vs Past Simple](/blog/grammar/present-perfect-vs-past-simple/).
pp-form.s: **have / has + past participle**: *I've finished. She hasn't called. Have you eaten?*
pp-form.b0.h: | I / you / we / they | he / she / it
pp-form.b1: The **past participle** of regular verbs ends in *-ed*, like the past simple: *work → worked, play → played*. Irregular verbs have their own form:
pp-form.b3: *He's* can mean *he is* or *he has*. If the next word is a past participle, it's *has*: *He**'s gone*** = he has gone. *He**'s going*** = he is going.
pp-form.w1: Use the past participle (been / gone), not the past simple.
pp-experience.s: Use the present perfect for **life experiences** up to now, without saying when: *Have you ever been to Canada? I've never tried sushi.*
pp-experience.b0: When we talk about experiences in our life (at any time up to now), we use the present perfect. We don't say **when**:
pp-experience.b1.1: ***Have** you **ever ridden** a horse?* (ever = at any time in your life)
pp-experience.b1.2: *She**'s never seen** snow.* (never = at no time)
pp-experience.b2: ***Ever*** is used in questions; ***never*** makes the sentence negative (don't add *not*): *I've **never** been there.* Not *I haven't never been there*.
pp-experience.b3: If you then give details (when, where, how), change to the **past simple**: *I**'ve been** to Rome. I **went** there in 2019 with my family.*
pp-experience.b4: *Been to* = went and came back (an experience). *I've been to Paris* = I visited Paris at some time in my life.
pp-experience.w2: With a past time: past simple
pp-just-already-yet.s: **just** = a short time ago; **already** = sooner than expected; **yet** = up to now (in questions and negatives, at the end).
pp-just-already-yet.b0.1.1: before now, maybe sooner than expected
pp-just-already-yet.b0.1.2: before the participle (or at the end)
pp-just-already-yet.b1: ***Yet*** in a question asks whether something we expect has happened. In a negative it means it hasn't happened, but we expect it to: *The bus **hasn't come yet**.*
pp-just-already-yet.b2: In American English, the past simple is also common with these words: *I **just ate**. Did you **finish yet**?* In British English, the present perfect is the usual choice. Both are correct.
pp-just-already-yet.w0: yet is for questions and negatives
pp-been-gone.s: *She's **gone** to Paris* = she's there now. *She's **been** to Paris* = she went and came back.
pp-been-gone.b0.0.1: She is at the bank now (or on the way).
pp-been-gone.b0.1.1: She went to the bank and she's back now.
pp-been-gone.b0.2.1: She visited Japan at some time in her life.
pp-been-gone.b1: Use ***gone*** when the person is **still away**. Use ***been*** when the person **has returned**, and for experiences.
pp-been-gone.b2: *Where have you been?* = you were away and now you're back. *Where has he gone?* = he isn't here now.
pp-result-news.t: A past action with a result now, and news
pp-result-news.s: The present perfect shows that a past action has a **result now** (*I've lost my keys* = I don't have them) and gives **new information**: *The prime minister has resigned.*
pp-result-news.b0: We often use the present perfect when a past action is important because of its **result now**:
pp-result-news.b1.0: *I**'ve lost** my keys.* (I can't get in now.)
pp-result-news.b1.2: *She**'s had** a haircut.* (Her hair looks different now.)
pp-result-news.b2: We also use it to give **news**: *The police **have arrested** a man in connection with the robbery.* When we add details (when, how), we usually switch to the past simple: *He **was arrested** at his home last night.*
pp-result-news.b3: Compare: *I**'ve lost** my keys* (I still haven't found them) and *I **lost** my keys yesterday, but I found them later* (finished story). See [Present Perfect vs Past Simple](/blog/grammar/present-perfect-vs-past-simple/).
pp-unfinished-time.t: Today, this week, recently, so far
pp-unfinished-time.s: Use the present perfect with periods of time that are **not finished**: *today, this week, this year, recently, lately, so far, up to now.*
pp-unfinished-time.b0: When the time period **includes now**, use the present perfect:
pp-unfinished-time.b2: Compare: *I**'ve seen** her **this morning*** (it's still morning) and *I **saw** her **this morning*** (it's now afternoon, the morning is finished).
pp-unfinished-time.b3: ***Recently*** can go with both tenses: *I**'ve recently started** yoga* / *I **recently started** yoga.* ***Lately*** usually goes with the present perfect.
pp-first-time-superlative.t: It's the first time… and the best… I've ever…
pp-first-time-superlative.s: After *It's the first / second time* and after a superlative + *ever*, use the present perfect: *It's the first time I've driven. It's the best film I've ever seen.*
pp-first-time-superlative.b0: When we talk about **now**, we use the present perfect after these patterns:
pp-first-time-superlative.b1.0: ***It's the first time** I**'ve eaten** sushi.* Not *It's the first time I eat sushi*.
pp-first-time-superlative.b1.1: *This is the **third time** he**'s been** late this week.*
pp-first-time-superlative.b1.3: *That was the **most boring** film I**'ve ever seen**.*
pp-first-time-superlative.b2: For a past situation, use the past perfect: *It **was** the first time I**'d** ever **flown**.* See [Past Perfect](/blog/grammar/past-perfect/#ppf-first-time).
pp-first-time-superlative.b3: *Ever* is optional with superlatives, but very common: *the best meal I've (ever) had*.

x.pp-been-gone-s02: She is still at the meeting: *gone*.

x.pp-experience-b03: Experience up to now: *have never flown*.
x.pp-experience-b04: *How many times* up to now: present perfect.
q.pp-just-already-yet-b02: In which sentence is the word order correct?
x.pp-just-already-yet-b08: *Yet* goes at the end of the question.
q.pp-been-gone-b03: *Tom has been to the supermarket.* Where is Tom now?
x.pp-been-gone-b05: You're back now: *Where have you been?*
x.pp-result-news-b02: News with a result now: *there has been*.
q.pp-result-news-b03: Which sentence gives news with a result now?
x.pp-result-news-b03: *Has risen* = new information with a result now.
x.pp-result-news-b04: News with a present result: *has hired*.
x.pp-result-news-b07: News with a result now: *has escaped*.
q.pp-unfinished-time-b03: It's 4 pm. Which sentence is correct?
x.pp-unfinished-time-b03: The morning is finished at 4 pm: past simple.
x.pp-unfinished-time-b04: *Recently* + a situation up to now: present perfect.
x.pp-unfinished-time-b05: This week isn't finished: *have you spent*.
x.pp-unfinished-time-b06: *So far* → present perfect (*team* can be singular or plural in British English).
